title: Kubernetes Internals
description: Understand kube-scheduler scoring, resource requests vs limits, QoS classes, Horizontal and Vertical Pod Autoscalers, and Pod Disruption Budgets.

segments.text: The kube-scheduler decides which node runs each pod using a two-phase algorithm. Filtering: eliminate nodes that can't run the pod — insufficient CPU, memory, or affinity violations. Scoring: rank remaining nodes by spread, resource balance, and custom priorities. The highest-scored node wins. Google runs clusters with fifteen thousand nodes, scheduling millions of pods daily.

Resource requests are guarantees — the scheduler ensures the node has that capacity. Limits are maximums — the kubelet kills the container if it exceeds memory limit. Set requests to your average usage and limits to your peak. Never set limits without requests — a pod with no request can be scheduled anywhere and starve other pods.

Kubernetes assigns QoS classes based on requests and limits. Guaranteed: requests equal limits for all containers — never killed for resource pressure. Burstable: requests set but lower than limits — killed after BestEffort pods. BestEffort: no requests or limits — first to be killed. Set Guaranteed for production workloads, Burstable for batch jobs.

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler scales replica count based on metrics. Default: CPU utilization above seventy percent triggers scale-up. Custom metrics: queue depth, request latency, or business metrics via Prometheus adapter. HPA has a cooldown period — default five minutes for scale-down — to prevent thrashing. Spotify scales thousands of services using HPA with custom metrics.

Your service has spiky traffic — idle for twenty-three hours, then one thousand requests per second for one hour. HPA scales up, but new pods take ninety seconds to start. Users experience errors during the scale-up window. How do you solve this?
segments.thought_prompt: How do you handle the HPA scale-up lag during sudden traffic spikes?

segments.text: Vertical Pod Autoscaler adjusts CPU and memory requests based on actual usage. It monitors historical consumption and recommends right-sized requests. VPA can run in recommendation-only mode — safer for production — or auto-update mode that restarts pods with new limits. Google uses VPA to save twenty to forty percent on compute costs by right-sizing over-provisioned pods.

Pod Disruption Budgets protect availability during voluntary disruptions — node drains, cluster upgrades, spot instance reclamation. A PDB specifying minAvailable two means Kubernetes won't evict pods if it would reduce available replicas below two. Without PDBs, a rolling cluster upgrade could evict all pods of a service simultaneously.

Advanced scheduling: node affinity pins pods to specific node types — GPU nodes for ML workloads. Pod anti-affinity spreads replicas across failure domains — no two replicas on the same node. Taints and tolerations reserve nodes for specific workloads — only ML pods on GPU nodes. Topology spread constraints ensure even distribution across zones.

Resource quotas prevent namespace resource hoarding. Set per-namespace limits on total CPU, memory, and pod count. LimitRanges set per-pod defaults and maximums — no pod can request more than eight CPUs. This prevents a single team from consuming the entire cluster. Google enforces strict quotas across their internal clusters with automated approval workflows.

Design the Kubernetes resource management strategy for a cluster running five hundred microservices across three availability zones. Define QoS classes, autoscaling, PDBs, and resource quotas for production, staging, and batch workloads.
segments.thought_prompt: Design K8s resource management for 500 services across 3 AZs: QoS, HPA, PDB, quotas.

segments.text: Kubernetes resource management is the foundation of reliable cluster operation. Requests and limits define QoS classes, HPA and VPA handle horizontal and vertical scaling, PDBs protect availability during disruptions, and quotas prevent resource hoarding. The Staff-level practice: always set requests equal to limits for production workloads to get Guaranteed QoS.
